_note: What the vacationing psychologists on the Florida beach say about the research (bd kge; dialogue/florida_psychologists.dialogue). Every line they speak carries a tag: [#cite=<id>] names a claim here, verified against its source, whose 'text' is the line's words exactly; [#author=<id>] names a line the author wrote, shipped as he wrote it, with the source text that supports it and what the sources do not show (author_lines); [#interp=<id>] names the psychologists' explanation, the author's rationale with no source (interpretations); [#chat] is their own talk. Sources are the site's citations page (Further reading) and the author's reference collection; no other literature is used. Claims are not quotes: a claim restates what the source's own text says, and 'evidence' holds that text.

_verification.method: SOP-06 adapted to claims, 2026-10-27: each claim and each support or gap quote was compared against the cited work's own text, fetched raw (not a model summary): the abstract from NCBI E-utilities (PubMed), the full text from PubMed Central where open (Porsch 2023), or the abstract in the DOI's Crossref record. 'evidence' and 'quote' are the source's sentences, '...' marking a gap between them. Interpretations and the author's own lines are not marked verified: no source states them as worded.
_verification.fields: claims: text, source, url (the DOI), aggregator, collection, population, checked_url, evidence, verified, checked_on, note (title when the work is in the author's references rather than on the citations page). author_lines: text, author_words, status, support (source, quote, statistic, population, verified), gap. interpretations: text, kind, author_words, note.
_verification.rule: A [#cite] line must be a verified claim; an [#author] line must have verified support and a stated gap; an [#interp] line is never presented as sourced (tests/test_florida_psychologists.gd).

vaillancourt2013_what.text: Indirect aggression includes criticizing a rival's looks, spreading rumors about someone's sex life, and leaving people out.

vaillancourt2013_females.text: A 2013 review says women and girls are particularly inclined to indirect aggression, and usually aim it at other women, especially attractive ones.

crick1995_measured.text: Older studies found boys more aggressive than girls. They had measured physical and verbal aggression.
crick1995_measured.source: Crick, N. R., & Grotpeter, J. K. (1995). Relational aggression, gender, and social-psychological adjustment. Child Development, 66(3), 710–722.
crick1995_measured.population: 491 children in grades 3 to 6; peer nominations and self-report
crick1995_measured.evidence: Prior studies of childhood aggression have demonstrated that, as a group, boys are more aggressive than girls. ... Overt aggression (i.e., physical and verbal aggression as assessed in past research) and social-psychological adjustment were also assessed.
crick1995_measured.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 7789197 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

crick1995_girls.text: In 1995 Crick and Grotpeter measured relational aggression in 491 children, third through sixth grade. The girls were significantly more relationally aggressive than the boys.
crick1995_girls.source: Crick, N. R., & Grotpeter, J. K. (1995). Relational aggression, gender, and social-psychological adjustment. Child Development, 66(3), 710–722.
crick1995_girls.population: 491 children in grades 3 to 6; peer nominations and self-report
crick1995_girls.evidence: In the present study, a form of aggression hypothesized to be typical of girls, relational aggression, was assessed with a peer nomination instrument for a sample of 491 third-through sixth-grade children. ... Further, they indicated that, as predicted, girls were significantly more relationally aggressive than were boys.
crick1995_girls.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 7789197 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

crick1995_adjust.text: And the relationally aggressive children were more rejected, and reported more loneliness, depression and isolation.
crick1995_adjust.source: Crick, N. R., & Grotpeter, J. K. (1995). Relational aggression, gender, and social-psychological adjustment. Child Development, 66(3), 710–722.
crick1995_adjust.population: 491 children in grades 3 to 6; peer nominations and self-report
crick1995_adjust.evidence: Results also indicated that relationally aggressive children may be at risk for serious adjustment difficulties (e.g., they were significantly more rejected and reported significantly higher levels of loneliness, depression, and isolation relative to their nonrelationally aggressive peers).
crick1995_adjust.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 7789197 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

vs2011_setup.text: In a 2011 experiment, women saw the same attractive woman dressed either conservatively or in a sexually provocative way.
vs2011_setup.source: Vaillancourt, T., & Sharma, A. (2011). Intolerance of sexy peers: Intrasexual competition among women. Aggressive Behavior, 37(6), 569–577.
vs2011_setup.population: two experiments with women participants; their reactions to a female confederate rated by independent raters blind to condition
vs2011_setup.evidence: Using independent raters, blind to condition, we found that almost all women were rated as reacting negatively ("bitchy") to an attractive female confederate when she was dressed in a sexually provocative manner. In contrast, when she was dressed conservatively, the same confederate was barely noticed by the participants.
vs2011_setup.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 21932332 (NCBI E-utilities raw text; the same abstract is in the Crossref record for the DOI).

vs2011_result.text: Dressed conservatively, she was barely noticed. Dressed provocatively, almost all the women were rated as reacting negatively to her.
vs2011_result.source: Vaillancourt, T., & Sharma, A. (2011). Intolerance of sexy peers: Intrasexual competition among women. Aggressive Behavior, 37(6), 569–577.
vs2011_result.population: two experiments with women participants; their reactions to a female confederate rated by independent raters blind to condition
vs2011_result.evidence: we found that almost all women were rated as reacting negatively ("bitchy") to an attractive female confederate when she was dressed in a sexually provocative manner. In contrast, when she was dressed conservatively, the same confederate was barely noticed by the participants.
vs2011_result.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 21932332 (NCBI E-utilities raw text; the same abstract is in the Crossref record for the DOI).

vs2011_rival.text: In a second study, women didn't want to introduce her to their boyfriends, leave him alone with her, or be friends with her.
vs2011_rival.source: Vaillancourt, T., & Sharma, A. (2011). Intolerance of sexy peers: Intrasexual competition among women. Aggressive Behavior, 37(6), 569–577.
vs2011_rival.population: two experiments with women participants; their reactions to a female confederate rated by independent raters blind to condition
vs2011_rival.evidence: In Study 2, an experimental design was used to assess whether the sexy female confederate from Study 1 was viewed as a sexual rival by women. Results indicated that as hypothesized, women did not want to introduce her to their boyfriend, allow him to spend time alone with her, or be friends with her.
vs2011_rival.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 21932332 (NCBI E-utilities raw text; the same abstract is in the Crossref record for the DOI).

The results showed that a high prevalence of involvement in cybergossip was associated with bullying and cyberbullying behavior (aggression and victimization), with girls showing the greatest involvement in cybergossip.

porsch2023_more.text: A 2023 review of ninety-nine papers: lesbian, bisexual and other sexual minority women are more likely than straight women to report violence from a partner.
porsch2023_more.source: Porsch, L. M., Xu, M., Veldhuis, C. B., Bochicchio, L. A., Zollweg, S. S., & Hughes, T. L. (2023). Intimate partner violence among sexual minority women: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 24(5), 3014–3036.
porsch2023_more.population: scoping review of 99 quantitative papers (2000 to 2021) on partner violence against adult sexual minority women; mostly survey (self-report) data
porsch2023_more.evidence: After independent reviewers screened these papers for relevance, 99 were included in the final review. ... Findings of this review provide additional evidence that SMW are more likely than heterosexual women to report IPV.
porsch2023_more.note: Compared against the full text, PubMed Central PMC10039964 (NCBI raw text), and the abstract, PubMed record 36154756.

porsch2023_perpetration.text: Most of the studies looked at victims. The review says emerging findings show perpetration is prevalent among these women, and understanding why is imperative.
porsch2023_perpetration.source: Porsch, L. M., Xu, M., Veldhuis, C. B., Bochicchio, L. A., Zollweg, S. S., & Hughes, T. L. (2023). Intimate partner violence among sexual minority women: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 24(5), 3014–3036.
porsch2023_perpetration.population: scoping review of 99 quantitative papers (2000 to 2021) on partner violence against adult sexual minority women; mostly survey (self-report) data
porsch2023_perpetration.evidence: the bulk of studies identified for this review focused on victimization ... given emerging findings that IPV perpetration is prevalent among SMW, it is imperative to better understand mechanisms underlying IPV among SMW, that is, why SMW may be aggressive with their partners
porsch2023_perpetration.note: Compared against the full text, PubMed Central PMC10039964 (NCBI raw text), and the abstract, PubMed record 36154756.

porsch2023_myths.text: It's hard to study. There are myths about whether women can be aggressive toward other women, and fear of stigmatizing sexual minorities even more.
porsch2023_myths.source: Porsch, L. M., Xu, M., Veldhuis, C. B., Bochicchio, L. A., Zollweg, S. S., & Hughes, T. L. (2023). Intimate partner violence among sexual minority women: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 24(5), 3014–3036.
porsch2023_myths.population: scoping review of 99 quantitative papers (2000 to 2021) on partner violence against adult sexual minority women; mostly survey (self-report) data
porsch2023_myths.evidence: It is important to note that there are unique challenges in studying IPV among SMW, such as differing perceptions and myths about women's ability to be aggressive towards other women, and fear of further stigmatization of sexual minority populations
porsch2023_myths.note: Compared against the full text, PubMed Central PMC10039964 (NCBI raw text), and the abstract, PubMed record 36154756.

porsch2023_understudied.text: In partner violence research, sexual minority women are understudied compared with straight women.
porsch2023_understudied.source: Porsch, L. M., Xu, M., Veldhuis, C. B., Bochicchio, L. A., Zollweg, S. S., & Hughes, T. L. (2023). Intimate partner violence among sexual minority women: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 24(5), 3014–3036.
porsch2023_understudied.population: scoping review of 99 quantitative papers (2000 to 2021) on partner violence against adult sexual minority women; mostly survey (self-report) data
porsch2023_understudied.evidence: However, compared to IPV research with heterosexual women and other LGBTQ+ population groups, SMW are understudied.
porsch2023_understudied.note: Compared against the full text, PubMed Central PMC10039964 (NCBI raw text), and the abstract, PubMed record 36154756.

porsch2023_risk.text: The risk factors the review found include prior trauma and victimization, substance use, and minority stressors like stigma and discrimination.
porsch2023_risk.source: Porsch, L. M., Xu, M., Veldhuis, C. B., Bochicchio, L. A., Zollweg, S. S., & Hughes, T. L. (2023). Intimate partner violence among sexual minority women: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 24(5), 3014–3036.
porsch2023_risk.population: scoping review of 99 quantitative papers (2000 to 2021) on partner violence against adult sexual minority women; mostly survey (self-report) data
porsch2023_risk.evidence: Risk factors for IPV in this population include prior trauma and victimization, psychological and emotional concerns, substance use, and minority stressors. ... SMW's risk of IPV is also likely affected by sexual minority-specific factors such as stigma, discrimination, internalized homophobia (IH), and concealment of sexual identities
porsch2023_risk.note: Compared against the full text, PubMed Central PMC10039964 (NCBI raw text), and the abstract, PubMed record 36154756.

hilton2024_measures.text: The measures and theories of coercive control mostly look at men coercing women.
hilton2024_measures.source: Hilton, N. Z., Ham, E., Radatz, D. L., Smith, C. M., Snow, N., Wintermute, J., Jennings-Fitz-Gerald, E., Lee, J., & Patterson, S. (2024). Coercive control in 2SLGBTQQIA+ relationships: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 25(5), 3713–3728.

hilton2024_measures.evidence: Existing measures and theories of intimate partner coercive control largely evaluate men's coercion of women.
hilton2024_measures.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 39066513 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

hilton2024_more.text: A 2024 review found coercive control was more common among Two Spirit and LGBTQ+ people, and related to mental health challenges.
hilton2024_more.source: Hilton, N. Z., Ham, E., Radatz, D. L., Smith, C. M., Snow, N., Wintermute, J., Jennings-Fitz-Gerald, E., Lee, J., & Patterson, S. (2024). Coercive control in 2SLGBTQQIA+ relationships: A scoping review. Trauma, Violence, & Abuse, 25(5), 3713–3728.

Coercive control was more common among minority individuals and was related to mental health challenges.
hilton2024_more.note: Compared against the article's abstract, PubMed record 39066513 (NCBI E-utilities raw text).

hilton2024_definition.text: And there's still no agreed definition of coercive control, or an accepted standard for measuring it.

sheppard2017_theory.text: A 2017 theory: people treat conflict between women at work as more of a problem than conflict between men, and that could exaggerate how badly women seem to get along.
sheppard2017_theory.source: Sheppard, L. D., & Aquino, K. (2017). Sisters at arms: A theory of female same-sex conflict and its problematization in organizations. Journal of Management, 43(3), 691–715.
sheppard2017_theory.population: theory paper, no new data: how third parties judge conflict between women and between men at work
sheppard2017_theory.evidence: we set aside consideration of possible gender differences in same-sex conflict frequency and draw from attribution theory to propose that female same-sex conflict is more problematized by third parties than male same-sex conflict, which could produce the exaggerated perception that women have more dysfunctional same-sex workplace relationships than men.
sheppard2017_theory.note: Compared against the article's abstract in the Crossref record for the DOI (raw JSON). A theory paper: the line says what it proposes, not a finding.

benenson2013_harm.evidence: Throughout their lives, women provide for their own and their children's and grandchildren's needs and thus must minimize their risk of incurring physical harm.

stockley2013_lowcost.text: Which fits with indirect aggression being a low-cost, effective way for young women to compete.
stockley2013_lowcost.source: Stockley, P., & Campbell, A. (2013). Female competition and aggression: interdisciplinary perspectives. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 368(1631), 20130073.
stockley2013_lowcost.population: introduction to an interdisciplinary theme issue on female competition and aggression in humans and other vertebrates
stockley2013_lowcost.evidence: Although female aggression takes diverse forms, under most circumstances relatively low-risk competitive strategies are favoured ... coalitions or alliances may reduce risk of retaliation. Consistent with these trends, indirect aggression is a low cost but effective form of competition among young women.

stockley2013_lowcost.title: Female competition and aggression: interdisciplinary perspectives

gap.quote: although rates of partner homicide were lower among lesbian couples than among gay male or heterosexual couples
gap.population: partner homicide; FBI Supplementary Homicide Reports (police data)
gap.reads: partner homicide rates in these police data: lower for lesbian couples than for gay male or heterosexual couples

gap.quote: Findings from studies using large U.S. probability samples suggest that bisexual women are significantly more likely than both heterosexual or lesbian women to report physical, sexual, and/or psychological IPV victimization
gap.population: large U.S. probability samples (surveys); bisexual, lesbian and heterosexual women; partner's gender not given
gap.reads: in the large surveys, bisexual women report the most, more than lesbian or heterosexual women

gap.quote: Thirteen studies compared the IPV prevalence among SMW and other SGM groups; findings from these studies are largely inconsistent.
gap.population: sexual minority women vs other sexual and gender minority groups, mostly men
gap.reads: comparisons of sexual minority women with other sexual and gender minority groups vary between studies

gap.quote: analyzed more than 2.5 million cases of IPV reported to law enforcement in the U.S. and found that female-female couples involved in these incidents were significantly younger than male-male and male-female couples
gap.population: IPV reported to U.S. law enforcement (police data)
gap.reads: this police-report study of couple types reports their ages, not their rates

The review measures violence against sexual minority women, mostly by survey, and mostly does not say the partner's gender; it does not compare rates between female same-sex, male same-sex and different-sex couples. No meta-analysis or police domestic-incident study comparing those rates was found in the sources checked (the citations page and the author's reference list). Renzetti (1992) is on the citations page; its text was not read.
